summary:
Two NASA instruments have watched fire for a quarter of a century. MODIS since 2000. VIIRS since 2012. But they don't see the same way. but VIIRS reports about four detections where MODIS reports one. Put their records together and fire in the United States seems to quadruple in 2012. The fires didn't change. The camera did.
So we made the two speak one language. For every fire VIIRS sees, we ask: would MODIS have seen it too? The heat of the fire gives the answer. The result is a single record, 2002 to 2025.
We stand on the shoulders of giants. Every method comes from published fire science: how to compare the two sensors (Wooster 2005, Schroeder 2014), how to group detections into fires (Balch 2020), how to find the land where stopping a fire matters most (Yemshanov 2021).
Everything lives in one web app. Search a place and press play to watch 24 years of fire move across the map. Click one of two million fires to see its danger level, its size and Landsat pictures before and after. Follow the satellites in orbit and see the ground they are scanning. Print a scientific report for any area, including the fires the satellites missed.
Pick any place. Pick any week. See it against its own history.
We are A Head Full of Dreams.
details:
What it does

Our app answers one question for any place in the United States: is this fire normal?

MODIS and VIIRS count fire differently, so we first made the two speak one language. For every fire VIIRS sees, we estimate whether MODIS would have seen it too, from the heat of the fire (a fire-radiative-power observation operator). That gives one record from 2002 to 2025, built from 13.4 million NASA FIRMS detections.

The page opens on the Earth with a play button. Press it and the globe opens on the United States. From there, one web app does five things:

  • Map. Search a place, press play, and watch 24 years of fire move across it. Unusual and record weeks are marked, and a year wheel shows the usual fire season.
  • Fires. Two million individual fires, each with its size, its duration and a danger level from Low to Extreme, in the colors of U.S. fire danger signs. Tested on years it never saw, the model scores AUC 0.936. For the larger fires: Landsat pictures before and after.
  • Satellites. Terra, Aqua, Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21 and Landsat 8 in 3D orbit, with the ground each one is scanning and its next pass over you.
  • Prevention. The land where a prescribed burn would cut the most likely paths of a wildfire.
  • Report. A printable scientific report for any states, counties or parks, with every table as a download.

Benefits and impact

A firefighter sees which new fire to look at first. A land manager sees where prevention pays off. A scientist gets a 24-year series without the false jump of 2012. And everyone sees the fires the satellites missed, because we compare our record with what agencies reported and show the gaps.

We want decades of NASA fire data to be something a person can use in a minute, without writing code.

How we built it

  • Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS), the MODIS burned-area, land-cover and tree-cover products, Landsat through Google Earth Engine, gridMET weather, SRTM terrain, agency wildfire reports, and CelesTrak orbit data.
  • Pipeline: Python, DuckDB and Parquet. The danger model is LightGBM, trained on 2012–2020 and tested on years it never saw.
  • Server: FastAPI on AWS Lightsail.
  • Web: plain JavaScript with MapLibre, D3, Observable Plot, three.js for NASA’s 3D satellite models, and satellite.js for the orbits.
  • Hardware: the whole pipeline runs on a laptop with under 5 GB of memory.

What makes it creative

We stand on the shoulders of giants. Each method comes from published fire science, and we turned each paper into something you can click: the sensor comparison (Wooster 2005, Schroeder 2014), the grouping of detections into fires (Balch 2020), and the prevention layer (Yemshanov 2021, Alexandridis 2008). The page reads like a fold-out guide map rather than a dashboard, with a first-visit tour and a 30-second tutorial video.

What we considered

  • Honesty. The app shows its own blind spots: fires before 2012 and fires in Hawaii have no danger level, and we say so.
  • Trust. The danger level is a suggestion of where to look first. It is not a dispatch order.
  • Plain language. Every screen is written for someone who has never heard of a hot spot, with readable contrast and keyboard use.
  • Openness. All code and methods are public in our repository.

We are A Head Full of Dreams.
